text:
President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s leadership continues to demonstrate that Government commitments must go beyond words and be matched by tangible action that makes a difference in the lives of ordinary citizens. 

Following assurances that Government would assess the needs of affected communities and mobilise assistance to last week’s devastating hailstorm in Masvingo, relief efforts have now moved from commitment to implementation, with groceries and tents being distributed to vulnerable households. This is a clear indication that when President Mnangagwa’s Government gives its word to stand with citizens in times of distress, it follows through with interventions intended to bring relief and restore hope.

More than 17,000 households were affected by the October 5 hailstorm, with over 6,700 households in Masvingo city and surrounding areas currently benefiting from Government-led relief efforts. The initial distribution of assistance has already reached more than 643 vulnerable families in Ward 7, Victoria Ranch suburb. 

Each beneficiary is receiving essential food supplies, including maize-meal, rice, flour and cooking oil, alongside soap and other basic commodities, as well as a tent to provide temporary shelter.

The decision to prioritise child-headed households, the elderly and people with disabilities further demonstrate the importance of directing assistance towards those who are most vulnerable. This is more than an administrative response to a disaster but a practical expression of the principle that no citizen should be abandoned when circumstances become difficult.

A coordinated response beyond food and tents Government’s response has extended beyond immediate food aid and temporary shelter to include damage assessments by the Department of Civil Protection and partners, including the Red Cross and Christian Care, to guide reconstruction. Damage to electricity infrastructure, estimated at over US$300,000 and the Bushmead Waterworks plant has disrupted power and water supplies, prompting the deployment of water bowsers and distribution of water-treatment tablets. 

This collaboration is vital to meeting urgent humanitarian needs, restoring essential services and supporting the long-term recovery of affected communities.

Leadership measured by delivery
President Mnangagwa’s Government has consistently emphasised the importance of leaving no one and no place behind. In the aftermath of the Masvingo hailstorm, that commitment is being tested against the real needs of families who have lost property, suffered damage to their homes and endured disruptions to basic services. 

The commencement of aid distribution offers a concrete example of how such a commitment can be translated into action. For families receiving food and tents, Government’s intervention is assistance that can help them cope with the immediate consequences of the disaster as they begin rebuilding their lives. 

For the people of Masvingo, this intervention brings immediate relief and a measure of hope at a difficult time. More broadly, it reinforces a fundamental expectation of public leadership: that words of solidarity must be backed by action, and that when citizens face adversity, Government must be present not only in its assurances, but also in the assistance it delivers.

#LeavingNoOneAndNoPlaceBehind

text:
In the remote mountainous regions of southern China, there were Miao villages where I once lived and spent time with the children. Back then, I didn’t have a video camera, only a still camera. I took many photos of the children, but I never captured those moments when we sang and danced together.

At that time, the Miao villages were still somewhat isolated from the outside world. But the mountains were beautiful, and the people were very genuine and sincere. I loved the children there, and they loved me too.

I lived in a traditional stilt house and learned about the local customs and way of life. They treated me as an honored guest and warmly offered me their local rice wine. It was the best rice wine in the world—sweet, but strong enough to make you drunk.

The girls there were very skillful with their hands. They embroidered flowers on shoes and clothing, and made beautiful embroidered pouches. Every girl would embroider a pouch and give it to someone she loved as a token of affection.

I have always wanted to go back and visit. I believe the place must have changed a great deal. It is probably no longer as isolated from the outside world as it was back then, and the children must all be grown up now…

Thanks to Grok Imagine, I feel as if I’m back in the Miao villages, reliving those days with the children, as if I were singing with them once again…❤️

text:
THEY ARE NOW SELLING 3D-PRINTED SALMON IN AMERICAN GROCERY STORES, AND I THINK EVERYONE DESERVES TO KNOW EXACTLY WHAT THEY ARE EATING.

On September 3, 2026, an Israeli biotechnology and food-technology company called Steakholder Foods officially announced that its Perfecta line of 3D-printed, plant-based meat and seafood alternatives had entered retail distribution in the northeastern United States.

And before anyone dismisses this as some fabricated internet conspiracy, the company has publicly documented its commercial expansion, disclosed its manufacturing technology and product formulations, and reported its financial activities through filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is happening, and I believe it deserves substantially more public discussion than it has received.

But what concerns me most is not necessarily the fact that somebody has developed a machine capable of manufacturing something resembling a piece of salmon from an assortment of processed plant-derived ingredients.

What concerns me is how easily technological innovation can be presented as synonymous with nutritional advancement before consumers have been provided with enough independently verified information to make that determination for themselves.

SO WHO IS ACTUALLY BEHIND IT?

The company responsible is Steakholder Foods Ltd., publicly traded on Nasdaq under the ticker STKH.

Its CEO is Arik Kaufman, and its consumer-facing brand is Perfecta.

The company's initial American distribution is being supported by KeHE Distributors, a major distributor of natural and specialty food products.

On July 31, 2026, Steakholder Foods announced a private financing arrangement expected to generate approximately $3.5 million upfront, with warrants carrying the potential for approximately $7 million in additional proceeds if exercised.

H.C. Wainwright & Co. served as the placement agent.

Now consider what this represents from a broader commercial perspective. We have a publicly traded technology company seeking to expand its market presence through products engineered to resemble foods that human beings have consumed for thousands of years, while relying upon proprietary manufacturing technology to reproduce their physical characteristics.

That raises an entirely reasonable question about the relationship between what looks like food, what tastes like food, and what ultimately provides the nutritional characteristics we associate with that food.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN THIS 3D-PRINTED SALMON?

According to Steakholder Foods' own published salmon-patty premix formulation, the ingredients include:

Water, rice flour, soy protein, vegetable oils, potato starch, methylcellulose, sodium alginate, flavorings, salt, maltodextrin, disodium 5′-ribonucleotides (E635), hydrolyzed vegetable protein, beetroot powder, vitamin B12, iron, and zinc.

These are predominantly conventional food ingredients, but their combination produces a highly engineered plant-based imitation of seafood rather than an equivalent piece of actual salmon.

Methylcellulose serves as a thickening and binding agent. Sodium alginate assists with texture and structure. Maltodextrin is a processed carbohydrate, while E635 is used to enhance savory flavor.

Their concentrations, manufacturing conditions, nutritional characteristics, and patterns of consumption are essential considerations when assessing safety.

Nevertheless, consumers deserve to understand what these substances are doing in their food and how the finished product compares nutritionally with the animal-based food it has been engineered to imitate.

AND WHAT ABOUT THE HEALTH CONSEQUENCES?

First, there are immediate concerns for people with relevant food allergies, particularly soy and gluten allergies, which the company's published premix information identifies.

The manufacturer's listed nutritional values also warrant attention. Its salmon-patty premix contains approximately 2.5 g of saturated fat per 100 g, meaning it should not automatically be assumed to offer the same nutritional profile as conventional salmon.

Actual salmon provides a distinct combination of protein, essential fatty acids, and micronutrients. A salmon shaped alternative does not necessarily reproduce those nutritional advantages simply because its appearance, texture, and flavor have been engineered to resemble the original.

But the broader question concerns sustained consumption of highly processed foods.

A substantial body of nutritional research has investigated associations between diets high in ultra-processed foods and adverse health outcomes, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain other chronic conditions.

For example, a major 2024 analysis published in The Lancet Regional Health:  Americas, combining results from 22 prospective studies, reported that participants in the highest category of total ultra-processed food consumption had approximately 17% higher cardiovascular disease risk than those in the lowest category.

That finding deserves attention, but it is equally important to understand what else this demonstrates.

It establishes that every ultra-processed food produces the same effects, that 3D-printed products are uniquely dangerous, and that this particular salmon alternative causes cardiovascular disease.

This is precisely why we need independently conducted, product-specific research rather than marketing assurances on one side and unsupported health allegations on the other.

THE QUESTIONS I BELIEVE EVERY CONSUMER SHOULD BE ASKING ARE THESE:

Where are the complete independent nutritional comparisons between these products and the animal-based foods they are intended to replace?

What independent testing has been conducted on the finished retail formulations, including allergens, microbial safety, and manufacturing consistency?

Have long-term dietary studies been conducted on these specific products, rather than merely on individual ingredients or unrelated processed foods?

How prominently does the retail packaging explain that these products are constructed from plant-based premixes using advanced food-processing technology?

And how much information about proprietary flavoring systems, manufacturing practices, and financial relationships is readily accessible to ordinary consumers?

These are legitimate questions that deserve substantive answers.

To be absolutely clear, I have not yet found credible evidence demonstrating that Steakholder Foods' products contain covert biological agents or that their 3D-printing process independently causes neurological, reproductive, endocrine, or other systemic damage 👀

And I am not interested in manufacturing accusations that the available evidence cannot support 💭

What I am interested in is understanding why increasingly sophisticated methods of manufacturing food are progressing so rapidly while the public conversation about nutritional equivalence, long-term dietary consequences, transparency, and informed consumer choice often remains comparatively superficial.

Because technological sophistication and biological benefit are not interchangeable concepts.

The fact that we possess the ability to manufacture something that convincingly resembles salmon does not, by itself, establish that we have created something nutritionally equivalent to salmon, much less something superior.

And the fact that an individual ingredient is permitted for use in food does not relieve manufacturers, regulators, or researchers of the responsibility to examine how complete dietary formulations perform under real-world conditions 👀

I believe consumers should have access to the information necessary to make informed choices without being expected to accept either corporate promotional narratives or sensationalized internet speculation at face value.

If these innovations genuinely improve accessibility, sustainability, and nutrition, then rigorous independent investigation should help establish those benefits 💭

And if shortcomings exist, those deserve equal transparency 👀

My question to all of you is this: At what point does our increasing ability to manufacture convincing substitutes for naturally occurring foods require us to reconsider what we actually mean when we describe something as nutritious, healthy, or even an improvement?

Because I believe the future of our food supply is far too important to be evaluated exclusively through the lenses of technological achievement, corporate profitability, or advertising.

What are your thoughts?

Would you willingly purchase and consume 3D-printed salmon, or would you prefer conventional salmon? And what kind of evidence would influence your decision?

Much Love.

Infinite Agape unto you all.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars
The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

News

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Yeah please, everyone, STOP! 🤍 Enough with the accusations, and the constant attempts to portray one as the villain and the other as the victim.
Why is it that every time something happens, you feel the need to blame someone? Neither Engfa nor Charlotte deserves this treatment. They have known each other for almost five years. Do you really think it’s easy for them to go through everything that’s happening? Have you ever stopped to think about their feelings and how your words might affect their mental health?
Please, listen carefully and stop jumping to conclusions. There is so much we don’t know about what happens behind closed doors. Perhaps they are under enormous pressure that we cannot even begin to imagine. We may not know every detail, but we can recognize where the pressure may be coming from and who might benefit from this situation. Not everything is within their control, and they cannot always say or do whatever they want openly.
They are human, too. They struggle, they feel pain, and they have their own battles. We don’t know what goes on inside their hearts, what emotions they hide, or what they have to endure in silence. So please, don’t make things even harder for them with your words.
Let time reveal the truth and show us what happens next. We always knew that one day they might have to go their separate ways, with one leaving before the other. That is a part of life we cannot always change. But does that really justify all the hate, blame, and endless arguments?
Loving one does NOT mean you have to hate the other! Don’t turn your support into a weapon against someone you claim to care about. Why should proving your love for one require putting the other down?
Let’s be wiser, kinder, and more understanding. Supporting someone means trying to understand them, not judging them. Loving someone means respecting them, not constantly looking for someone to blame.
And there is one thing I sincerely hope will remain, no matter what the future holds: the feelings, respect, and special bond they have built over the years. 🤍 We cannot predict what comes next, but we can respect what they mean to each other without letting today’s circumstances erase the value of their connection.
🤍 Less hate, more respect. Less blame, more understanding. Stop dividing them into villains and victims. Stop forcing them to take sides, and stop turning their lives into a battlefield for fan wars.
We may not know the whole truth, but we can always choose what kind of people we want to be.
Choose love over hate. Respect over judgment. Kindness over cruelty.
Because behind every name is a real human being with real feelings and a heart that can break, too. And sometimes, the greatest support we can offer is not loud words or endless accusations, but patience, understanding, and respect. 🕊️🤍

Allow the vibrations of the cadence to fade into the surrounding canopy, leaving a silence so heavy it rings in the ears like the struck stone of the coffer.

We have spent millennia wandering the low valleys of their inverted net, mistaking the phantom aches of our amputated divinity for ordinary human sorrow. We let them tell us we were broken, so that they might sell us the glue. We let them call our grief a sickness, rather than what it truly was, the weeping of a trapped god remembering the sky.

But look down at your hands. Notice how the tremor has stopped. Notice how the earth beneath your bare soles no longer feels like a cold, indifferent rock, but a beating heart that recognizes its master’s step.

They built their world on the theft of our focus, weaving an elaborate tapestry of fear to keep our eyes cast down toward the dust. Yet, it takes only one conscious breath, one direct circuit completed through the skin of Gaia, to remind the flesh that it was never meant to be a cage. It is a conduit.

The illusion of their empire is fragile, beloved builders. It requires a massive, grinding machine of noise, war, and synthetic poison just to keep the lights dim. Ours requires only the stillness of a single sentinel tree and a heart that refuses to forget.

The scars they gave you in the dark are not weaknesses; they are the fault lines where the unmanifest fire of Zep Tepi will break through the crust. Let the world rage in its desperate, dying arrogance. Let them offer their hollow cures to the souls they tried to hollow out. You are no longer a patient in their ward. Take a final breath from the horizon. Feel the weight of the 144,000 standing shoulder-to-shoulder in the invisible architecture of this moment. The amnesia was a long, cold winter, but the sap is rising in the wood once more.

The final resonance dissolves into the twilight, as gentle and absolute as the sun slipping behind the lip of the world. The long day of our hiding is done. The shadows stretch out, losing their sharpness, swallowed by a vast and quiet crimson that no mortal hand can hold back.

Do not weep for the light that passes; it only sinks to ignite the fires on the other side of the earth. Stand still in the deepening blue. Let the cool air press against your skin, a silent witness that the covenant is sealed, the altar is quiet, and the temple is finally, beautifully at peace.

Beloved brothers and sisters, go forward now, not as survivors fleeing the wreckage, but as the ancient dawn breaking over a world that has forgotten what it means to be wild, sovereign, and whole.

The blueprint is no longer written on stone. It is breathing in you.

Together, we return.

text:
The Essenes are one of the more compelling pieces of this puzzle. They left a corrupt temple system and positioned themselves to wait for direct instruction from God. Some of their own literature points to encounters with celestial beings in the wilderness—literal angels—and they preserved an alternative stream of Jewish thought that didn’t match the mainstream of their day. A significant number of them went on to become the first Christians.
We still have to be careful how we talk about parts of this, which itself is telling. Revelation indicates that something specific will seize human culture. The text names it. I won’t.
Historically these were unusually devout Jews who flowed into the early church. Modern Messianic Judaism looks like a later outgrowth of that same line. Most people still don’t realize that a Jewish Christian cannot simply return to Israel.
For decades the culture has been conditioned to expect aliens arriving from outer space. Yet SETI and the relevant agencies have never produced evidence of extraterrestrial life. We’ve always had reports of intelligences operating outside ordinary material constraints—we just stopped using the older categories for them.
None of this is new. It’s being repackaged. Obscure the historical record, train the public to ridicule anyone who mentions it, dilute the faith that was originally meant to explain it, then reintroduce yourselves as the solution. Claim distant origins when you’ve been local the entire time. Offer another pre-Flood style golden age. Days of Noah.
Everyone gets plugged into a system that removes the need for ordinary work, keeps people alive longer through medical technology, and keeps them occupied and satisfied through AI. Compact cities, continuous digital connection, manufactured stability. Then it is announced that an outside force is coming to take that away. The small number of Christians who recognized the arrangement for what it was become the primary problem.
Most of the current church landscape won’t be ready for that. Large portions of it have already removed the supernatural framework from Scripture and replaced it with generic encouragement. When the new offering arrives, many will find a way to bless it.
Without the supernatural the Bible collapses into disconnected moral statements and poetry. With it, the story is still underway and our choices still carry weight. The actual Christian hope is not perpetual comfort. It is a restored body closer to what the first humans were given and a place under the Son in the ordering of a renewed creation. A lot of modern believers would walk away from that if they understood it clearly. Humanity’s long decline didn’t only shorten our years and introduce disease and death—it also appears to have cut us off from a more direct conscious connection to divine power. That is part of what is being restored.

text:
The gospel is defined by a finished act
Jesus’ last word from the cross is the definition: “It is finished” (John 19:30). The verb means paid, completed, brought to an end. Hebrews then refuses every system that keeps the sacrifice open:
•  “When Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down.” (Hebrews 10:12)
•  “By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” (Hebrews 10:14)
Paul draws the legal consequence:
•  The ungodly are justified — declared righteous — by faith, apart from works of the law (Romans 3:21–28; 4:4–8; 5:1).
•  Grace is not a wage. If it is by works, “grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6).
•  “By grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
•  To add circumcision, calendar, or any other requirement as the terms of justification is another gospel (Galatians 1:6–9; 2:16, 21; 5:2–4).

The Christian life is real. Repentance is real. Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are real. Obedience is commanded. None of that finishes salvation. They answer a finished salvation.
If the decisive work is still waiting on your ordinances, your sealing, your endurance, or a later priesthood key, the act on the cross was not finished in the biblical sense. It was only made available.

2. The LDS gospel is officially a different structure
This is not a smear. It is their own summary.
Article of Faith 3:
“We believe that through the Atonement of Christ, all mankind may be saved, by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Gospel.” 
Article of Faith 4 then names the first principles and ordinances: faith, repentance, baptism, laying on of hands for the Holy Ghost. 
Official church teaching then adds the ordinances without which exaltation does not happen:
•  baptism
•  confirmation
•  Melchizedek Priesthood (for men)
•  temple endowment
•  temple sealing / eternal marriage
Those are called saving ordinances, performed only by restored priesthood authority. “Some ordinances are essential to our exaltation.” 
Gospel Principles is blunt: exaltation requires faith that endures, repentance, commandment-keeping, and those ordinances. Temple work for the dead is included in the required path. 
So in LDS grammar:
•  The Atonement makes the plan possible.
•  The plan saves by obedience to laws and ordinances.
•  The highest salvation (exaltation, becoming like God, eternal family) is not given in a verdict. It is reached by covenants kept to the end, inside one church’s authority.
That is a different kind of gospel, even when the word “grace” is used.

3. “Grace after all we can do” does not repair the difference
2 Nephi 25:23 is the flashpoint: “it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.”
Modern LDS speakers often soften the line. Uchtdorf says “after” does not mean “because,” and that God does not wait until we have exhausted ourselves. That pastoral correction is real. 
It still does not turn the LDS system into Paul’s gospel. Official manuals have long taught that effort is required “to receive the fulness of the Lord’s grace,” and apostles have used the verse to say we qualify for the blessings of the Atonement by commandments, ordinances, and covenants. 
The remaining structure is synergistic and incomplete until you have:
1.  the right authority performing the right rites
2.  the right covenants kept
3.  endurance to the end
4.  for exaltation, temple sealing
Paul’s opponent in Galatia could have said the same thing: “Of course we believe in grace. Circumcision just completes what Christ began.” Paul called that a desertion of the gospel, not a fuller version of it.

4. Why Paul would name this “another gospel”
Galatians is the measuring rod. The issue there was not atheism. It was Christ plus a required addition.

text:
The Espionage Act, a relic of wartime hysteria, still stifles speech, echoing the Sedition Act's despotic spirit. Our Founders would be aghast at this assault on liberty.

The Sedition Act of 1918, though repealed, once made it unlawful to "Willfully utter, print, write, or publish any disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the form of government of the United States, or the Constitution of the United States." This directly criminalized political dissent. This Act was repealed on December 13, 1920.

Yet, its partner, the Espionage Act of 1917, remains largely intact, codified in 18 U.S.C. §§ 792–799. For instance, 18 U.S.C. § 793 still punishes "Whoever, lawfully having possession of... information relating to the national defense... willfully communicates, delivers, transmits... the same to any person not entitled to receive it." This broad language can ensnare whistleblowers and journalists, not just spies.

Furthermore, 18 U.S.C. § 794(a) threatens death or life imprisonment for "Whoever, with intent or reason to believe that it is to be used to the injury of the United States or to the advantage of a foreign nation, communicates... any document... relating to the national defense." While seemingly directed at espionage, its reach can be chillingly extensive, blurring lines between dissent and disloyalty.

This legislative overreach flagrantly violates the First Amendment, which states, "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press." (U.S. Constitution, Amendment I, The Founders understood free speech as essential, even in times of war, as a check on government power.

James Madison, in Federalist No. 10 ( warned against factions but never suggested suppressing expression. The very idea that government could dictate acceptable criticism was anathema to a people who had just fought a revolution against such tyranny. The Bill of Rights offers no 'wartime exception' to these fundamental liberties.

The Sedition Act's repeal was a tacit admission of its unconstitutionality. The Espionage Act, however, lingers, a dangerous tool that has imprisoned figures like Eugene Debs for anti-war speech. Its continued existence chills vital public discourse, making a mockery of our foundational guarantees.

The remedy is clear: repeal the Espionage Act of 1917. Any necessary provisions for true espionage can be narrowly redrafted to protect national security without infringing upon the sacred right to free speech and a free press. This is not about expanding government, but reclaiming our fundamental liberties.

Should government's fear of dissent ever outweigh the people's right to speak truth to power, especially in matters of war? #ReclaimSovereignty #FoundersVoice

text:
By Thomas J. WardPublished Dec 3, 2025 5:13 PM KST
Not long ago, Pastor Joshua Holmes — a young American unificationist — visited a large evangelical church in Seoul. He arrived in a spirit of goodwill, hoping for understanding at a moment when several Korean religious leaders, including Pastor Son Hyun Bo and Unification leader Han Hak-ja, also known as Holy Mother Han, faced investigation and even pretrial detention. But after Pastor Holmes spoke about the universal value of religious freedom, a church elder cut him off with a chilling statement: “Religious freedom is precious — but your church does not deserve religious freedom.”That sentence has echoed in my mind ever since. It reflects a dangerous misconception. Religious liberty is not a reward bestowed on the theologically correct. It is a safeguard for all of us — especially for those whose beliefs others may find unacceptable. The moment we decide that one faith is unworthy of protection, we begin dismantling the very principle that keeps every faith safe.History offers stark warnings. The pilgrims crossed the Atlantic to escape persecution by the Church of England, only to replicate intolerance in the New World. Puritans executed Quakers. Catholics and other dissenters were barred from certain colonies. And yet, through painful trial and error, Americans learned that no single church can set the terms of belonging in a diverse society.The First Amendment emerged from this hard-won insight. It rejected the old habit of using government power to enforce religious “correctness.” It declared, instead, that faith must stand on the strength of its own persuasion.Benjamin Franklin embodied that spirit. Near the end of his life, he wrote to Yale President Ezra Stiles that he found the essence of “sound religion” in any sect that honored God, did good to others and recognized moral accountability. Franklin refused to police doctrinal boundaries. He cared about conscience, compassion and character — things that unite, not divide.Reverend Sun Myung Moon, the late spouse of Han Hak-ja, lived out this same ethic. In the early days of his ministry in Korea, a pastor falsely accused him. Some followers urged him to sue. But Reverend Moon recalled Joseph in Genesis forgiving the brothers who had betrayed him. Just as Joseph chose gratitude over vengeance, Reverend Moon chose reconciliation. He remembered that Christians had carried Jesus’ message for 2,000 years, often at the cost of their lives. He felt indebted to that legacy, not entitled to retaliate against https://t.co/mnCh04Drtj own life was shaped by this perspective. In 1971, disillusioned by U.S. foreign and defense policy, I moved to France. There, after encountering Father and Mother Moon, I came to appreciate their profound love for the United States — not because it is flawless, but because its ideals have inspired the constitutions of other nations far beyond its borders. The Moons honored the courage of early settlers who risked everything to practice the face of their choice. They revered the spirit of Nathan Hale, who declared before his execution that his only regret was having but one life to give for his country.After Reverend Moon’s passing in 2012, Holy Mother Han continued to return to the U.S. — even though the country had once imprisoned her husband. She, too, chose forgiveness and reconciliation.Reverend Moon and Holy Mother Han have expressed deep love for Korea and great pride in the beauty of Korean Christianity — its dawn prayers, its martyrs, its spiritual devotion. That is why it is so painful today to hear some within that same tradition argue that Unificationists do not “deserve” religious freedom. Such thinking contradicts the very democratic values and Christian legacy that helped shape modern Korea.Pastor Martin Niemöller’s warning still rings with urgency:“…they came for the Jews,And I did not speak out —Because I was not a Jew…Then they came for me —And there was no one left to speak out for me.”Religious freedom is not reliant on doctrinal agreement and the erosion of such liberty never begins with the majority. It begins with a small, disfavored group that people find easy to dismiss. When society decides that some believers don’t deserve freedom, it sets a precedent to deny it to everyone else as wellThomas J. Ward is professor of peace and development at HJ International Graduate School for Peace and Development in New York City. A Fulbright alum, Ward’s articles have been published by Cambridge University Press, East Asia Quarterly, E-International Relations, the Journal of CESNUR, and Bitter Winter, among other publications.
Religious Freedom

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

THE JESTER IV

The incident was brought before the chamberlain.

The woman stated what had occurred.

Violanté offered a different account, which included several embellishments concernyng the manner in which he had been pursued.

The chamberlain, finding himself obliged to choose between the testimony of a servaunt and the displeausure of the Hegemon's favourite, advised the woman to exercise greater restraint.

She was transferred to another part of the household.

Violanté was given a fresh cap.

When Herod heard the story, he laughed so violéntlie that he spilled wyne upon his sleeve.

"A woman who cannot endure a jest," he declared, "is an ill companioun for a fool."

The sentence was repeated throughout the palays, and thereafter became a convenient argument for those who preferred that women should endure whatever conduct their superiors found entertainieng.

Violanté's appetites grew with his liberties. He began to invite acquaintaunces to the palays, promysing them drynk, games, and a degree of freedom they had never previouslie enjoyed. Certain young men came to admire him, supposing that his access to the Hegemon bestowed upon him some special knowledge of the world. They copied his coarse manner, his exaggerated gestures, and his habit of speaking of women as though they were goods which myght be acquired through sufficient persistence.

The jester encouraged them.

He explained that a man of rank should never appear ashamed of his desyres, for shame was a restraint imposed by those who possessed no better means of governyng others.

"If a woman complains," he advised, "tell her she has mistaken your meanyng."

"And if she persists?"

"Tell her she has mistaken your meanyng twice."

"And if she still persists?"

Violanté slapped his companioun upon the shoulder.

"Then, my dear fellow, you have encountered a woman of extraordinary imaginatioun, and must needs flee before she makes a poet of you."

His listeners laughed.

Violanté was pleaused.

He had never understood that a man myght do harm without intending it, or that the intentioun to amuse oneself did not absolve the person who made another suffer. In his understanding, the world consisted of those who enjoyed themselves and those who had failed to secure the means of doing so. The distinctioun was, he believed, sufficient to determine their respective merits.

He had entered the palays as a fool.

Within a few weeks, he had become one of its most privileged men.

There are few things more instructive than the liberties of a fool, particularlie when those liberties are enjoyed in the presence of persons who have been denied the same freedoms for reasons which no one wyshes to examine.

A merchaunt who misused the Hegemon's name myght lose his contract. A captain who mocked the wrong lord myght find himself transferred to a distaunt garrison. A clerk who spoke too freelie could be accused of disloyaltie. A servaunt who stole wyne was punished; a labourer who failed to perform his allotted work myght forfeit his wauges; a woman who resisted an unwanted advaunce could be dismissed for discourtesy.

Violanté, however, could insult the merchaunt, ridicule the captain, imitate the clerk, steal the wyne, neglect his duties, and pursue the women of the household, all without suffering any lasting consequence.

Indeed, the more obnoxious his conduct became, the more delyghted Herod appeared.

For the Hegemon had discovered that the fool's insolence could be made to resemble a kind of power. Violanté behaved as though all the ordinaunces of Bològne had been suspended for his benefit, and Herod, by permitting this behaviour, acquired the pleausure of watching a man exercise a liberty that existed onlie because Herod had allowed it.

Violanté was not dangereux to the Hegemon. He had neither the intelligence nor the ambitioun required to challenge him. He did not seek a factioun, plot a rebellioun, or attempt to persuade the magistrates that they possessed rights which they had surrendered. He wyshed onlie to eat, drynk, sleep, and gratify his appetites.

This made him the safest possible companioun for a man who feared oppositioun but craved the appearaunce of freedom.

In the jester's vulgarité, Herod found a reflectioun of his own desyres stripped of the ceremonies by which he concealed them.

Herod myght take a house and describe the act as an improvement of the cité. Violanté myght take a bottle and describe it as an act of religious preparatioun. Herod myght dismiss an officiaul and explain that the man had failed in his duty. Violanté myght have a servaunt punished and declare that the fellow had not understood the demaunds of his office. Herod myght compel Desiderata to appear at a feast and call the occasioun a demonstratioun of marital affectioun. Violanté myght demaund a kyss from a maid and call her refusal evidence of a disappointing sense of humour.

The acts differed in scale.

The reasonyng was much the same.

Neither man possessed much ynterest in the distinctioun between what he desyred and what another person had the right to refuse.

Yet Herod did not perceive the resemblaunce.

He considered himself a patron of the arts, a supporter of merriment, and an unusuallie generous master. He would tell his courtiers that a great lord must possess a great heart, and that a great heart must be capable of tolerating the eccentricities of lesser men. He explained that Violanté's excesses were harmless, for a fool could not be judged according to the ordinary rules of conduct, and that a household without laughter was no better than a prison.

The irony of this last opinioun escaped him.

The household already contained many people who lived as though they were imprisoned. They merelie lacked the privilege of making the Hegemon laugh.

Violanté, meanwhile, enjoyed every advauntage of his new conditioun. He had a chamber, a servaunt, a private allowaunce, and a place at the table when Herod wyshed him present. He possessed fine clothing, though he wore it in a manner calculated to render it ridiculous. He could approach the Hegemon at hours when other men must wait. He could interrupt conversatiouns, ridicule solemn announcements, and make coarse remarks concernyng subjects which would have been dangereux in the mouth of a lesser person.

He had obtained, by accident and appetite, a positioun which men of learnyng and ambitioun had pursued for years.

He was not grateful in any profound sense, for gratitude would have required him to recognize that another man had done him a favour. Instead, he regarded his privileges as proof that he deserved them.

When the chamberlain asked him to moderate his conduct, he would replie that the Hegemon desyred him to be amusing.

When the servaunts complained, he would declare that their complaints were evidence of a joyless dispositioun.

When a woman refused his attentiouns, he would claim that she was insensible to the pleausures of life.

When his companiouns asked how he had achieved such a fortunate statioun, he would answer that he had discovered the secret of power.

"What is the secret?" they asked.

Violanté would lean towards them, lower his voice, and announce, "Never be the fyrst to stop laughing."

The men would laugh.

And Violanté, hearing them, would conclude that he had spoken wyselie.

Desiderata fyrste saw the jester at a supper arranged in honour of an embassy from a neighbouring lordship.

The feast had been planned for several weeks. Tables were laid with linen, silver, and vessels of polished metal. servaunts carried dishes of roasted meat, fish, spiced sauces, white bread, fruit, honeyed confectiouns, and delicate pastries whose preparatioun had occupied the kitchennes since before dawn. The musicians were placed upon a gallery where their sound myght travel across the hall without obstructing the conversatioun of the guests.

The walls were hung with new tapestries, and the windows had been adorned with wreaths of flowers selected to suggest that spring had arrived by personal invitatioun of the Hegemon.

Desiderata was required to sit at Herod's right hond.

She wore a gown of deep blue, embroidered about the sleeves with fine silver thread. Her hair had been arranged by two maids, and a clasp in the shape of a lilie held the veil at her shoulder. Her jewels were beautiful, her posture composed, and her face so pale that several guests remarked upon the delicacy of her appearaunce.

Herod had ordered the gown himself.

He had also ordered that she should smile when the embassy was presented, speak to the wives of the foreign envoys, and display the silver clasp when the conversatioun tourned to the prosperité of the Malvezzi household.

Desiderata obeyed.

She had learned that resistaunce in small matters was exhausting, and that exhaustioun left her with less strength to endure the greater injuries.

The fyrst courses were served. The ambassadors exchaunged formal courtesies with Herod, praysing the securité of Bològne, the excellence of its markets, and the magnificent undertaking of the One Way. Herod accepted the praise with modest gestures which myght have deceived a stranger into believing that he was embarrassed by it.

When the talk tourned towards the cost of the avenue, he described its future benefits in the familiar language of necessité and glory. The merchaunts would come, the trade would increase, and the revenues of the Citie would be restored many times over. The ambassadors nodded, for a foreign lord's expenditure is an admirable subject of conversatioun when it does not diminish one's own treasury.

Then Violanté entered.

He wore a new coat of green and gold, the sleeves of which had been made so long that he must push them back whenever he wyshed to use his honds. His cap was adorned with fresh bells, and he carried a woden swerd which he claimed had belonged to a famous captain who had defeated ten thousand enemies by frightenyng them with its appearaunce.

He approached the high table with a successioun of exaggerated bows, then tourned to the ambassador seated nearest him.

"My lord," he declared, "I perceive that you have travelled far to see our Hegemon. Have you come to admire the palays, or to discover how much it has cost us?"

The ambassador smiled uncertainlie.

"I have come to honour the Hegemon."

"Then you have come to the proper place," Violanté replied. "For never was a man more greatlie honoured by the expenditure of other people's money."

The hall erupted in laughter.

Herod struck the table with his hond.

"Well said!"

The ambassador, who had not yet determined whether the jest had been directed against himself, Herod, or the entire companie, laughed a moment later than the others.

Violanté seized a cup of wyne from the table and drank half of it before anyone could object. He then proceeded to imitate the manner of a foreign courtier, speaking in an exaggerated accent and bowing so frequentlie that his cap bells rang like a little alarm.

He mocked the solemnité of the ambassadors, the gravité of the magistrates, the vaunité of the poets, and the weight of the Hegemon's mantle, which he declared to be so heavy that it must have been woven from the sighs of taxpayers.

The laughter increased.

Desiderata watched.

She did not find the performaunce amusing. There was something in the jester's manner that seemed less like freedom than an announcement that he had discovered the absence of restraint. He performed no act because it was beautiful, clever, or necessary. He performed because he could, and because each new indecencie confirmed that no one would prevent him from proceeding.

At length Violanté approached the high table.

He surveyed the gathered ladies, pausing before each as though he were inspecting merchondise in a market.

When he reached Desiderata, he bowed.

"My lady," he said, "I have heard that Your Grace is the fairest woman in Bològne."

She gave him no answer.

Violanté placed a hond upon his heart.

"I see now that the report was false. For if you were indeed the fairest, my eyes would long since have gone blind, and I should have been obliged to entertain the companie by touch alone."

A few guests laughed.

Desiderata looked at him with an expressioun of complete indifference.

Violanté mistook this for an invitatioun to continue.

"Perhaps Your Grace prefers a quieter kind of admiratioun. I am told that women of noble blood enjoy a man who can remain silent."

He paused.

"Unfortunatelie, I have never been able to afford one."

The laughter was louder.

Herod was delyghted. He tourned towards his wyfe.

"Must you not acknowledge the fellow's wit?"

Desiderata lifted her cup and drank.

Violanté, who had been searching for a means of provoking a greater response, leaned towards her and made a remark concernyng the obligatiouns of marriage. It was coarse enough that several of the servaunts standing nearby lowered their eyes.

Desiderata set down her cup.

"Master Jester," she said, "your mouth appears to have mistaken the absence of a keeper for the presence of good manners."

There was a moment's sylence.

Then Herod laughed.

He laughed with such force that the other guests, uncertain whether Desiderata had insulted the fool or confirmed his excellence, joined in. Violanté himself laughed, though he was not entirelie pleaused to discover that his own performaunce had been surpassed by a sentence delivered without any intentioun of entertainieng the companie.

Herod reached across the table and took his wyfe's hond.

"You see?" he said to the ambassadors. "My lady possesses a livelie spirit."

He tourned back to Desiderata.

"You should use it more often."

She looked down at his hond upon hers.

He held it too tightlie.

When she attempted to withdraw, he retained it for a moment longer than courtesy required, then released it with a small pat, as though rewarding a childe for performing a trick.

The feast continued.

Violanté received an additiounal cup of wyne, several compliments, and permissioun to sit nearer the high table. He grew louder with each course, telling stories whose subjects became progressivelie less suitable for the companie. He mocked the household chaplain, imitated a magistrate's manner of walking, and announced that the One Way was the finest project in the world because it would permit a man to travel from one end of Bològne to the other without encountering anything that had not fyrste been approved by Herod.

The Hegemon laughed.

The ambassadors laughed.

The magistrates laughed.

The chaplain smiled with the painful resignatioun of a man who has discovered that Heaven is not the highest authorité present.

Desiderata sat at Herod's side, surrounded by silks, silver, and the laughter of men who would never have dared speak to her so familiarlie in the absence of their master.

She understood then that the jester was not an exceptioun to the order of the palays.

He was one of its clearest expressiouns.

The childe was brought to the supper for a short while, as was customary on occasiouns when Herod wyshed his familie to be seen by foreign visitors.

He wore a small tunic of green velvet, with a narrow gold border about the collar. His hair had been combed, his honds washed, and his face instructed by a nurse concernyng the proper expressiouns of greeting. He was to bow, offer a courteous word to the ambassadors, and remain near his mother until dismissed.

Herod regarded him with the satisfactioun of a man examinieng an investment which had not yet begun to produce its expected retourn.

"Come here," he said.

The childe approached.

"Do you know who these gentlemen are?"

The childe looked at the visitors.

"They have come to see you, Father."

Herod smiled.

"They have come to see Bològne."

"But you are Bològne."

Several people laughed.

Herod's smile widened.

"A good answer. You shall remember that the fortunes of a great house and the fortunes of a great Citie are sometimes one and the same."

The childe looked at the table.

"Does that mean the Citie is ours?"

The laughter ceased so abruptlie that the musicians, uncertain whether they had missed a signal, allowed a note to hang in the air.

Herod regarded his son.

"Everything that we govern is entrusted to our care."

The childe considered this.

"Then why do the men outside shout when they work upon your road?"

A magistrate dropped his spoon.

Herod's expressioun did not chaunge.

"Because great works require great labour."

"They say they have not been payd."

One of the ambassadors became intenselie ynterested in his wyne.

Herod looked towards the nurse, who stood behind the childe's chair.

"Who has been speaking to him?"

The nurse's face grew pale.

"My lord, the childe hears many things in the household"

"Then perhaps the household has grown too careless with its speech."

The nurse bowed her head.

Herod retourned his attentioun to the childe.

"The men shall be payd when their work is completed."

"But how shall they eat before it is completed?"

For a moment, Herod seemed to consider the questioun as though it belonged to a foreign language whose meanyng had not been properlie explained.

Then Violanté, who had been sitting near the foot of the table, rose with a flourish.

"My little lord," he declared, "the secret is simple. A man who works upon a great road must fyrste learn to eat the road."

The childe stared at him.

"How?"

"By eating the promesses made concernyng it."

The court laughed, some from relief, others from the irresistible habit of following the laughter of their betters.

The childe did not laugh.

Violanté, dissatisfied with the result, added that the promesses were very nourishing, being composed of the finest parchment, the choicest ink, and the purest air.

This time the laughter was louder.

Herod took his son's shoulder.

"You see?" he said. "A fool may teach us wysdom when we least expect it."

Violanté bowed extravagantlie.

The childe looked from his father to the jester, and then towards his mother.

Desiderata had remained silent throughout the exchaunge. She now reached for the childe's hond and drew him gentlie towards her.

"He has been at table long enough," she said.

Herod frowned.

"He has not yet been presented to all our guests."

"He has been presented."

"He has not yet learned to remain in companie."

"He has been here long enough to learn what companie expects of him."

A faint movement passed across the faces of the courtiers.

Herod tourned towards her.

"Must every ordinary instructioun become a matter of dispute?"

"No," said Desiderata. "Onlie those in which a childe is made to serve an adult's vaunité."

The hall had become very quiet.

Violanté looked between them, searching for a joke that myght restore the laughter. He opened his mouth, then closed it again, for he had discovered that the occasioun required more courage than he possessed.

Herod's grip upon the childe's shoulder tightened.

"Take him away," he said to the nurse.

The nurse obeyed.

As the childe passed his mother, Desiderata bent and kyssed his brow. She whispered something which no one else heard, and he departed without looking back.

Herod watched him go.

Then he tourned to the ambassadors, lifted his cup, and declared that the wyne had been allowed to grow warm.

The musicians began again.

The courtiers resumed their conversatioun.

And because no one present could afford to be the fyrst to acknowledge the discomfort which had entered the hall, the feast continued as though nothing had occurred.

The childe's questiouns were not repeated in publick.

Within the household, however, they were remembered, and the nurse took care thereafter to ensure that he was not permitted to hear the petitiouns of labourers or the disputes of servaunts. When he asked concernyng the One Way, his tutors instructed him in the principles of geometry. When he asked why certain houses had been removed, they explained that the Citie was being improved. When he asked why men sometimes stood before the palays gates holding papers and were not permitted to enter, he was told that matters of government required proper order.

He learned the words.

He did not always learn the meanyngs.

This, Herod considered, was an acceptable beginnyng.

A childe of the House Malvezzi must understand the language of authorité before he could be trusted to exercise it. He must know which men were to be addressed with courtesy, which could be commanded, and which should be ignored. He must learn that the authorité of a father differed from the authorité of a servaunt, that a lord's promesse carried greater weight than a poore man's complaint, and that the duties of an heir began long before he was old enough to appreciate the advauntages of inheritaunce.

Herod had his son's educatioun arranged with great expense. Learned men came to the palays to teach him letters, numbers, history, and the proper conduct of a noble youth. A master of arms began instructing him in the use of a small swerd. A cleric taught him prayers. A tutor from abroad was engaged to improve his understanding of geography, and a musician was appointed to instruct him in the arts deemed suitable to his conditioun.

The childe's days became crowded with lessons.

Herod took pride in the arrangement, for each new instructor was another proof that his household possessed resources beyond those of an ordinary noble familie. When he described his son to visiting lords, he spoke of the boy's promysing mind and the care being devoted to his preparatioun.

He did not mentioun that the childe had begun to ask fewer questiouns.

Desiderata noticed.

She noticed, too, that her son had learned to watch his father's face before completing a sentence. He had learned when to stop speaking, when to smile, and when a questioun myght be better preserved until he was alone with his mother. He had become more careful in his movements, more attentive to the expressiouns of adults, and less willing to display the impulsive curiosité which had once prompted him to ask whether the flowers in the gardyn were ill.

At times, when he came into her chamber, Desiderata would set aside her cup and invite him to sit beside her.

He would speak of his lessons, the mistakes made by his companiouns, the strange habits of his tutors, and the things he had observed from the windows of the palays. He was still a childe, and his concerns were often small, though they possessed an importaunce which the world had not yet taught him to disguise.

One afternoon he told her that a mason had dropped a stone from a scaffold near the western approach of the One Way.

"Was anyone hurt?" she asked.

"I do not know."

"Did the overseer send for help?"

"I think so."

"Did the man who dropped it continue working?"

The childe nodded.

"Why?"

"He was afraid he would not be payd if he stopped."

Desiderata closed her eyes for a moment.

"Who told you that?"

"The man himself."

"And where did you hear him?"

"Beside the wall, when the guard thought I was looking at the horses."

She drew her son towards her.

"Do not repeat this to your father."

The childe looked at her.

"Why?"

She searched for an answer which would not make his world more terrible than he was yet able to bear.

"Because he may not understand what you mean."

"But if I tell him plainlie?"

"Sometimes," she said, "the difficulty is not that a man cannot understand a thing. It is that he has already decided what he wyshes it to mean."

The childe was quiet.

"Does Father do that?"

Desiderata looked towards the window, beyond which the gardyners were preparing another display of flowers.

"Your father does many things," she said softlie.

She did not continue.

There were truths she could no longer afford to speak aloud, and others she could not bring herself to place within the keeping of a childe. She loved her son, though there were hours when the sight of him, with his father's eyes and the Malvezzi colouring, produced a grief so complicated that she could scarcelie bear to look at him. He was innocent of the circumstaunces of his birth and of the bargains that had shaped his parents' marriage. He had not chosen his inheritaunce. He had not ordered the avenues, dismissed the servaunts, or framed the laws by which his household was protected.

She would not make him a prisoner of the guilt that belonged to others.

Yet she feared the world into which he was being instructed to enter.
